newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - July 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - July 3.

text.p: MPs turn on Peters over Winebox: Prime Minister Jim Bolger parried accusations in Parliament on Wednesday that Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters had perjured himself during the Winebox inquiry. Page 1.

'Solid support' needed to move Beehive: Before moving the Beehive and completing Parliament Buildings in the original Edwardian style, the government would have to be convinced New Zealanders really wanted this, Foreign Affairs Minister Don McKinnon said on Wednesday. Page 1.

Delamere retracts redneck allegation: Associate Treasurer Tuariki Delamere has withdrawn allegations that police showed redneck attitudes in investigating the theft of a Colin McCahon painting. Page 2.
Tariff removal plan 'driven by ideology': The government's plan to speed up the removal of tariffs continued to draw criticism on Wednesday. Page 15.

NZ pressured over smuggling: Incident dropped after Chinese counterpunch: Chinese officials retaliated to this year's apple-smuggling scandal by accusing New Zealanders of stealing plant material from China.
Govt blocks bid by NZ Post to expand: The government is believed to have blocked New Zealand Post's intended bid for the express freight businesses put up for sale by Freightways.
Sky confident of doubling subscribers: Sky Network Television is confident of doubling its subscribers over the next few years but is refusing to say exactly when it expects to break even.
Fast move to sell property SOE: The government has moved swiftly to act on its budget vow to sell Government Property Services, one of two SOEs earmarked for sale.
Ostrich venture buries its head: Failed ostrich investment concern Savannah Ostrich Processing Company owed unsecured creditors $376,000 when it was put in the hands of liquidators in May.

Telecom quickly taps line into competitive advantage: Telecom on Wednesday launched PCS BusinessZone, the first of a new generation of cellular-cumlandline products aimed at giving it a competitive edge in an increasingly commodised market for its core business.

NZ 'poorly-prepared' for important agricultural negotiations in 1999: New Zealand is not well enough prepared for the coming World Trade Organisation negotiations on agriculture says a former trade ambassador to the United Kingdom, Brian Chambertin.
Farmers angry over virus ruling: Frustrated South Island farmers reacted angrily to the decision on Wednesday to reject the rabbit calicivirus disease. Page 1.

GPs raise concerns over free child consultations: General practitioners are worried that the government's newly announced free consultations for children under the age of six will hurt their own pockets. Page 4.
Faster payments lift Smiths: Customers paying their accounts faster have helped Smiths City Group post a higher profit despite difficult trading. Page 30.
